name: Abu Bakr
line: The Prophet's closest friend, the first free man to believe, and the first caliph.
story: A respected Makkan merchant, he believed the moment he was invited and was called al-Siddiq for confirming the Night Journey. He spent his wealth freeing tortured slaves like Bilal. He hid with the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Thawr during the Hijrah. As caliph for two years he held Arabia together and began gathering the Quran.
legacy: His steadiness after the Prophet's death kept the young community united.
lesson: True friendship means standing by the truth when others doubt it.
note: 9:40 speaks of the 'second of two' in the cave, understood by all commentators as Abu Bakr. 24:22 was revealed about him and his relative Mistah (Reported by al-Bukhari, in the hadith of the slander). One of the ten promised Paradise.
title: Caliph

name: Umar ibn al-Khattab
line: A fierce opponent who became Islam's great strength, and the caliph who built its state.
story: Umar set out to harm the Prophet ﷺ but found his sister reciting the Quran and became Muslim around 616. After that, Muslims prayed openly at the Kaaba. As caliph for ten years he opened Syria, Iraq, Egypt and Jerusalem, set up the Hijri calendar, courts and stipends, and walked the streets at night checking on the poor.
legacy: Much of how Muslim government works, from the calendar to public treasury, began with him.
lesson: Power is a trust: the ruler answers for every hungry person in his land.
note: Umar said his opinion matched later revelation in three things: the station of Ibrahim (2:125), the veil (33:53) and 66:5 (Bukhari 402). He was stabbed while leading the dawn prayer in 644. One of the ten promised Paradise.
title: Caliph

name: Uthman ibn Affan
line: A gentle, generous merchant who married two of the Prophet's daughters and gave the Ummah one Quran.
story: Uthman was among the first to believe and migrated to Abyssinia with his wife Ruqayyah. He bought the well of Rumah for the people of Madinah and equipped the army of Tabuk. As caliph for twelve years he sent copies of a single agreed Quran to the cities. He was killed in his home in Madinah in 656, reading the Quran.
legacy: Every printed Quran today follows the Uthmanic copy.
lesson: Modesty and generosity are a strength, not a weakness.
note: Called Dhul-Nurayn, 'the one with two lights', for marrying Ruqayyah and then Umm Kulthum. The Prophet ﷺ said the angels feel shy before him (Muslim 2401). One of the ten promised Paradise.
title: Caliph

name: Ali ibn Abi Talib
role: Fourth caliph, the Lion of Allah
line: The Prophet's young cousin, the first boy to believe, husband of Fatimah and fourth caliph.
story: Raised in the Prophet's own house, Ali believed as a boy and slept in the Prophet's bed on the night of the Hijrah. He carried the banner at Khaybar and was famed for courage, knowledge and plain living. He became caliph in a time of deep division after Uthman's death, and was struck down in Kufa's mosque in 661.
legacy: Father of Hasan and Husayn; his sayings and judgements shaped Muslim law and wisdom.
lesson: Knowledge and humility belong together.
note: The Prophet ﷺ told him, 'You are to me as Harun was to Musa, except there is no prophet after me' (Bukhari 3706). One of the ten promised Paradise. Killed by the Kharijite Ibn Muljam.
title: Caliph

name: Talhah ibn Ubaydullah
line: An early believer who shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his own body at Uhud.
story: Talhah accepted Islam through Abu Bakr in the first days. At Uhud, when the Prophet ﷺ was exposed, he stood in front of him and caught arrows with his hand until it was crippled. He was known for open-handed charity, earning the name Talhah of goodness. He died in 656 at the Battle of the Camel.
note: His crippled hand from Uhud is reported by al-Bukhari. One of the ten promised Paradise (Tirmidhi 3747). The civil strife of 656 is a matter on which Sunni scholars hold back from blaming any Companion.

name: Al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam
line: The Prophet's cousin, whom he called his own disciple, like the disciples of Isa.
story: Son of the Prophet's aunt Safiyyah, Zubayr became Muslim as a teenager and is said to be the first to draw a sword for Islam. He fought in every major battle and married Asma bint Abi Bakr. Later he served in the conquest of Egypt. He was killed in 656 after leaving the field before the Battle of the Camel.
note: 'Every prophet has a disciple (hawari), and my disciple is al-Zubayr' is reported by al-Bukhari. One of the ten promised Paradise.

name: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf
line: A Makkan who arrived in Madinah with nothing, asked for the market, and became rich and generous.
story: When the Ansari Sa'd ibn al-Rabi offered him half his wealth, Abd al-Rahman thanked him and said, 'Show me the market.' Trading honestly, he grew wealthy and gave much of it away for the army and the poor. Umar named him to the council of six that chose the next caliph, and he oversaw the choice of Uthman.
note: 'Show me the market' is reported by al-Bukhari. The Prophet ﷺ once prayed behind him at Tabuk (Reported by Muslim). Death year given as 652 or 654. One of the ten promised Paradise; he narrates the hadith naming them.

name: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
line: An early convert whose mother's hunger strike brought down verses on duty to parents.
story: Sa'd accepted Islam at about seventeen. His mother refused to eat until he left it; he answered that even a hundred lives would not change him. He was the first to shoot an arrow for Islam. Under Umar he led the army that defeated Persia at Qadisiyyah and founded Kufa. He kept out of the later civil strife.
note: That 29:8 and 31:15 were revealed about Sa'd and his mother is reported by Muslim. Death year given between 671 and 675. One of the ten promised Paradise.

name: Sa'id ibn Zayd
role: Son of a seeker of truth
line: An early believer whose father searched for the religion of Ibrahim before Islam.
story: His father Zayd ibn Amr refused idols and sought the faith of Ibrahim, dying before the Prophet's mission. Sa'id and his wife Fatimah, Umar's sister, were Muslims when Umar burst in on them; their recitation helped turn Umar to Islam. He fought at Yarmuk and lived quietly near Madinah.
note: One of the ten promised Paradise; he also narrates a version of the hadith of the ten (Reported by Abu Dawud). Death year given as 671 to 673.

name: Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah
line: The man the Prophet ﷺ called the trustworthy one of this Ummah.
story: Abu Ubaydah became Muslim early and fought at Badr and Uhud, where he pulled two links of armour from the Prophet's cheek with his teeth. Umar gave him command in Syria, where he took Damascus and Jerusalem's surrender was arranged. When plague struck at Amwas he refused to leave his soldiers and died among them in 639.
note: Some commentators link 58:22 to Abu Ubaydah, who faced his own father at Badr; this is from tafsir, not certain. One of the ten promised Paradise.

name: Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib
role: Lion of Allah, master of martyrs
line: The Prophet's strong uncle, whose conversion made Quraysh think twice.
story: Hamzah, a hunter and warrior, heard that Abu Jahl had insulted his nephew and struck him with his bow, declaring his Islam. He fought in the first duels at Badr. At Uhud in 625 he was killed by a spear thrown by Wahshi, and the Prophet ﷺ grieved deeply over him.
note: That 22:19 was revealed about the Badr duel of Hamzah, Ali and Ubaydah ibn al-Harith is reported by al-Bukhari. The title 'master of martyrs' comes from a narration in al-Hakim.

name: Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib
line: The Prophet's uncle, keeper of Zamzam water for pilgrims, and forefather of the Abbasid caliphs.
story: Abbas protected his nephew at the Aqabah pledge though not yet openly Muslim. He was taken captive at Badr, ransomed, and openly joined Islam around the conquest of Makkah, standing firm at Hunayn. In a drought, Umar prayed for rain through his supplication. He died in Madinah around 653.
legacy: The Abbasid dynasty took its name from him.
note: Commentators say 8:70 was addressed to the Badr captives including Abbas; this is from tafsir. When exactly he became Muslim is debated.

name: Jafar ibn Abi Talib
line: Ali's elder brother, who spoke for the Muslims before the Christian king of Abyssinia.
story: Jafar led the Muslim refugees in Abyssinia. When Quraysh demanded them back, he explained Islam to the Najashi and recited from Surah Maryam, and the king wept and protected them. He returned in 628 and was killed commanding at Mu'tah in 629, losing both arms while holding the banner.
lesson: Speak the truth plainly and gently, even before kings.
note: He recited the opening of Surah Maryam to the king. His speech to the Najashi is reported by Ahmad from Umm Salamah. He is called Dhul-Janahayn, 'the one with two wings', given him in Paradise in place of his arms (Reported by al-Bukhari).

name: Bilal ibn Rabah
line: An Abyssinian slave tortured for his faith, who became the first caller to prayer.
story: His master Umayyah ibn Khalaf laid him on burning sand with a rock on his chest, but Bilal only repeated, 'One, One.' Abu Bakr bought and freed him. In Madinah his voice called the first adhan, and on the day Makkah opened he gave the call from the roof of the Kaaba. He later moved to Syria and died in Damascus.
lesson: In Islam, rank comes from faith, not colour or birth.
note: The Prophet ﷺ heard Bilal's footsteps ahead of him in Paradise (Bukhari 1149). Death year given as 640 to 642.

name: Sumayyah bint Khayyat
line: A former slave woman, the first person killed for being Muslim.
story: Sumayyah, her husband Yasir and son Ammar were among the earliest Muslims in Makkah. Because they had no tribe to protect them, they were tortured in the open sun. Sumayyah refused to give up her faith and was killed by Abu Jahl around 615, becoming the first martyr of Islam.
lesson: Faith can be stronger than the cruellest power.
note: 'Be patient, family of Yasir, your promised place is Paradise' is reported by al-Hakim and others. Her father's name is also given as Khabbat.

name: Yasir ibn Amir
line: A Yemeni settler in Makkah, tortured to death with his wife for Islam.
story: Yasir came to Makkah from Yemen and stayed under the protection of the Makhzum clan, marrying Sumayyah. When the family became Muslim they had no one to defend them and were tortured in the heat. Yasir died from the torment soon after his wife.

name: Ammar ibn Yasir
line: Tortured until he spoke words of disbelief, he was comforted by a verse from the Quran.
story: Ammar saw his parents killed for their faith. Under torture he finally said what Quraysh demanded, then came to the Prophet ﷺ in tears. He was told that if his heart was firm, he was excused. In Madinah he helped build the first mosques. Umar made him governor of Kufa. He died at Siffin in 657, aged over ninety.
lesson: Allah judges the heart, and does not burden a soul beyond what it can bear.
note: That 16:106 was revealed about Ammar is the report of Ibn Abbas in tafsir. He fought on Ali's side at Siffin.

name: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt
line: A Makkan blacksmith burned with hot coals for his faith, and a teacher of the Quran.
story: Khabbab was among the first six or so Muslims. His owner pressed him onto burning coals. When he asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for help, he was told that believers before had been cut with saws and combed with iron combs and stayed firm. He was teaching the Quran in Fatimah bint al-Khattab's house when Umar arrived. He died in Kufa.
note: 19:77-80 were revealed about al-As ibn Wail, who refused to pay Khabbab what he owed (Reported by al-Bukhari).

name: Al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam
line: A young convert whose house near Safa became the secret meeting place of the first Muslims.
story: In the hardest years in Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ taught the believers in al-Arqam's house beside Mount Safa, away from the eyes of Quraysh. Many early Muslims, by some reports Umar too, came to Islam there. Al-Arqam later fought at Badr and lived on in Madinah.
note: His death year is given as 673 to 675.

name: Mus'ab ibn Umayr
line: A wealthy, well-dressed youth of Makkah who left everything and became Islam's first teacher in Madinah.
story: His mother cut him off when he became Muslim. In 621 the Prophet ﷺ sent him to Yathrib, where he taught the Quran so well that the leaders of the Aws and Khazraj accepted Islam. He carried the banner at Uhud and was killed there. He owned so little that his cloak could not cover both his head and feet.
lesson: One sincere teacher can open a whole city.
note: The short shroud of Mus'ab is reported by al-Bukhari from Khabbab. Some commentators include him among those meant by 33:23.

name: Uthman ibn Maz'un
line: An early, deeply devout believer, the first Muhajir to die and be buried at al-Baqi.
story: Uthman ibn Maz'un migrated to Abyssinia, then returned and gave up a pagan's protection so he could suffer with the other Muslims. He wanted to give up marriage to devote himself to worship, but the Prophet ﷺ forbade it. He died in Madinah around 625, and the Prophet ﷺ kissed him and wept.
lesson: Islam asks for balance, not extremes, even in worship.
note: The Prophet ﷺ forbidding him celibacy is reported by al-Bukhari. The kiss is reported by al-Tirmidhi. Death year given as 624 or 625.

name: Suhayb al-Rumi
line: Raised among the Byzantines, he gave all his wealth to Quraysh to be allowed to emigrate.
story: Captured as a boy and raised in Byzantine lands, Suhayb came to Makkah as a freed man and grew rich. When he tried to leave for Madinah, Quraysh blocked him, so he handed over all his wealth. The Prophet ﷺ greeted him: 'Your trade has profited.' Umar chose him to lead the prayers while the new caliph was chosen.
note: Several commentators say 2:207 was revealed about Suhayb; others make it general.

name: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari
line: A desert man who walked to Makkah to find the Prophet ﷺ, famous for honesty and plain living.
story: From the tribe of Ghifar, Abu Dharr declared his Islam out loud at the Kaaba and was beaten for it. He went home and brought much of his tribe into Islam. He asked for a governorship but was told he was too gentle for it. Strict about wealth, he spent his last years in the desert at al-Rabadhah.
lesson: Leadership is a trust, not a prize.
note: His conversion story is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

name: Salman al-Farisi
line: A Persian who left his home to search for the truth and found it in Madinah.
story: Born a Zoroastrian near Isfahan, Salman became a Christian and served a line of monks, the last of whom told him a prophet would appear in Arabia. Sold into slavery, he reached Madinah and recognised the signs. At the Battle of the Trench he suggested digging the ditch. He later governed al-Mada'in, the old Persian capital.
lesson: A sincere search for truth is never wasted.
note: When 62:3 was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ put his hand on Salman and said men of his people would reach faith even if it were at the Pleiades (Bukhari 4897). The long life sometimes given to him in later sources is not reliable.

name: Fatimah bint al-Khattab
line: Umar's sister, whose courage and recitation turned her brother to Islam.
story: Fatimah and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd were secret Muslims. When Umar heard and stormed into their house, he struck her, but she stood firm and told him she would never leave Islam. Shaken, Umar asked to read the page they had, verses of Surah Ta-Ha, and went from there to the Prophet ﷺ to become Muslim.
lesson: A quiet believer's firmness can change a giant.
note: The page held the opening of Surah Ta-Ha (20:1-8). The story is told by Ibn Ishaq and others; details vary between reports.

name: Umm Ayman
line: The Abyssinian woman who cared for the Prophet ﷺ from birth, whom he called his mother after his mother.
story: Barakah, known as Umm Ayman, was with Aminah when she died and raised the orphaned boy. The Prophet ﷺ freed her, honoured her all his life and married her to Zayd ibn Harithah; their son was Usamah. She emigrated to both Abyssinia and Madinah. After his death, Abu Bakr and Umar visited her, and she wept that revelation had stopped.
note: The visit of Abu Bakr and Umar is reported by Muslim. 'My mother after my mother' is from the biographers. Her death date is given variously, under Abu Bakr, Umar or Uthman.

name: Asma bint Abi Bakr
line: Abu Bakr's daughter, who carried food to the cave during the Hijrah.
story: During the Hijrah, Asma tore her waistband in two to tie up the food she carried to the Prophet ﷺ and her father in the cave of Thawr, earning the name Dhat al-Nitaqayn. She married al-Zubayr and was mother of Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr. She lived to about a hundred and died in Makkah in 692, days after her son.
lesson: Courage and loyalty do not depend on age.
note: The two belts story is reported by al-Bukhari. When her pagan mother visited, she was told to keep good ties with her (Reported by al-Bukhari); some reports connect 60:8 to this.

name: Asma bint Umays
line: An early believer who emigrated to Abyssinia with Jafar and was told she had two hijrahs.
story: Asma went to Abyssinia with her husband Jafar ibn Abi Talib and stayed there for years. When Umar teased the returning emigrants that the Madinans had more right to the Prophet ﷺ, she complained, and he said they had two migrations. After Jafar's death she married Abu Bakr, and after him Ali.
note: The 'two hijrahs' hadith is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

name: As'ad ibn Zurarah
line: One of the first men of Yathrib to believe, who hosted Islam's first teacher there.
story: As'ad met the Prophet ﷺ at the pilgrimage season and pledged at Aqabah. He hosted Mus'ab ibn Umayr in Yathrib and went with him from house to house, bringing chiefs like Sa'd ibn Mu'adh to Islam. He led the first Friday prayers there, and died within the first year after the Hijrah, before Badr.
note: That he led the first Friday prayer in Madinah is reported by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah.

name: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh
line: The Aws chief whose death, the Prophet ﷺ said, made the Throne of Allah shake.
story: Sa'd came to Islam through Mus'ab, then told his clan he would not speak to them until they believed, and they all did. Before Badr he told the Prophet ﷺ the Ansar would follow him even into the sea. Wounded by an arrow at the Trench, he was nursed in Rufaydah's tent, judged the case of Banu Qurayzah, and died in 627.

name: Sa'd ibn Ubadah
line: The generous chief of the Khazraj, whose house fed the poor of Madinah.
story: Sa'd pledged at Aqabah and became one of the leaders of the Ansar, famed for hospitality. He carried a banner of the Ansar on the day Makkah was opened. After the Prophet's death the Ansar gathered at his Saqifah, the roofed hall where Abu Bakr was chosen. He later moved to Syria and died in Hawran around 636.
note: His death year is given between 635 and 637.

name: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari
line: The Madinan whose house the Prophet's camel chose, and who died in old age before Constantinople.
story: When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, his camel knelt by Abu Ayyub's home, and he lived there until his own rooms were built. Abu Ayyub fought in every campaign he could. In his eighties he joined the army besieging Constantinople, fell ill, and asked to be buried as close to its walls as possible.
legacy: His tomb in Istanbul is one of the most visited in the Muslim world.
note: His death is given between 669 and 674. The Ottomans later built the Eyup mosque at his grave.

name: Abu Talhah al-Ansari
line: A skilled Ansari archer who gave his favourite garden away when a verse was revealed.
story: Abu Talhah married Umm Sulaym, who accepted Islam as her only dowry. At Uhud he shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his shield and arrows. When 3:92 told believers they would not reach righteousness until they spent from what they love, he gave away Bayruha, his best date garden. He died around 654.
lesson: Give from what you love most.
note: The night his family went hungry to feed a guest, after which 59:9 was revealed, is reported by al-Bukhari; Muslim names the host as Abu Talhah. Some say he died at sea on campaign.

name: Ubayy ibn Ka'b
line: A scribe of revelation, so fine a reciter that Allah named him to the Prophet ﷺ.
story: Ubayy, an Ansari who could read and write, wrote down revelation in Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ told him that Allah had commanded him to recite Surah al-Bayyinah to Ubayy, and Ubayy wept, asking, 'Did He name me?' Umar appointed him to lead the night prayers of Ramadan in congregation.
note: His death year is disputed, given anywhere from 640 to 656.

name: Zayd ibn Thabit
line: The young scribe who wrote the Quran for the Prophet ﷺ and later gathered it into one book.
story: Too young for Badr, Zayd served instead with his pen, writing revelation and learning other scripts for the Prophet's letters. After many memorisers died at Yamamah, Abu Bakr asked him to collect the Quran; he said moving a mountain would have been easier. He later led the committee that made Uthman's standard copies.
legacy: The written Quran in every Muslim home passes through his hands.
note: His learning of the Jewish script is reported by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi. Death year given between 660 and 676.

name: Mu'adh ibn Jabal
line: A young Ansari scholar whom the Prophet ﷺ loved and sent to teach and judge in Yemen.
story: Mu'adh accepted Islam as a teenager and became known for knowing what is lawful and unlawful. Sending him to Yemen, the Prophet ﷺ asked how he would judge; he answered by the Quran, then the Sunnah, then his own reasoning. The Prophet ﷺ walked beside his mount in farewell. He died in the plague of Amwas in 639.
note: The 'how will you judge' dialogue is reported by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi; many hadith scholars consider its chain weak though its meaning is widely accepted.

name: Anas ibn Malik
line: Given as a boy to serve the Prophet ﷺ, he served ten years and lived past a hundred.
story: Umm Sulaym brought her son Anas, about ten, to the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah. In ten years, Anas said, he never once said 'uff' to him or asked why something was done. The Prophet ﷺ prayed for his wealth, children and long life. He settled in Basra, narrated over two thousand hadith, and was among the last Companions to die.
note: Death year given between 709 and 712.

name: Umm Sulaym bint Milhan
line: An Ansari woman whose only dowry was her suitor's Islam, and whose patience became a byword.
story: Umm Sulaym gave her son Anas to serve the Prophet ﷺ. When Abu Talhah proposed, she said his Islam would be her dowry. When their little son died, she calmly fed her husband and only then told him, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed for their night; they were blessed with a son. At Hunayn she carried a dagger.
note: The dowry story is reported by al-Nasa'i; the death of her son by al-Bukhari and Muslim; the dagger at Hunayn by Muslim. Her death date is not known.

name: Umm Haram bint Milhan
role: First woman to sail for Islam
line: The woman the Prophet ﷺ foresaw sailing with the first Muslim fleet, who died on Cyprus.
story: The Prophet ﷺ napped at Umm Haram's house and woke smiling: he had seen Muslims riding the sea like kings on thrones. She asked to be among them, and he said she would be. Decades later she joined the first naval expedition, to Cyprus in 649, fell from her mount and died there.
legacy: Her shrine, Hala Sultan Tekke near Larnaca, still stands.

name: Nusaybah bint Ka'b
role: Shield of the Prophet at Uhud
line: Known as Umm Ammarah, she fought around the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud when most had scattered.
story: Nusaybah was one of two women at the second pledge of Aqabah. At Uhud she came to bring water, but when the line broke she took up a sword and shield to defend the Prophet ﷺ, and was wounded many times. Years later, in the battle of Yamamah, she lost a hand.
lesson: Courage is not only for men.
note: Al-Tirmidhi reports that 33:35 came after Umm Ammarah asked why the Quran mentioned only men (hasan gharib); a similar question is also reported from Umm Salamah. Her battle accounts come from the biographers.

name: Rufaydah al-Aslamiyyah
line: A woman who ran a tent by the Prophet's mosque to care for the wounded.
story: Rufaydah was skilled in treating wounds and set up a tent beside the mosque in Madinah. When Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was struck by an arrow at the Trench, the Prophet ﷺ had him moved to her tent so he could visit him often. She is remembered as the first nurse in Islam.
note: Her tent is mentioned by Ibn Ishaq. Little else about her life, including her dates, is certain.

name: Al-Shifa bint Abdullah
line: One of the few literate women of Makkah, who taught writing and healing.
story: Al-Shifa could read and write when few could. The Prophet ﷺ asked her to teach Hafsah the healing charm she knew, as she had taught her writing. Umar respected her advice. She lived in a house the Prophet ﷺ gave her in Madinah.
note: Teaching Hafsah is reported by Abu Dawud. The report that Umar put her in charge of the market is found in later biographies and is disputed.

name: Umm al-Fadl Lubabah
line: Among the first women to accept Islam, mother of Ibn Abbas.
story: Lubabah bint al-Harith, wife of al-Abbas, is said to be the second woman after Khadijah to accept Islam. Her sister Maymunah became a wife of the Prophet ﷺ. On the day of Arafah, when people wondered whether he was fasting, she sent him a cup of milk and he drank it in front of them.
note: The milk at Arafah is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim. 'Second woman to believe' is from the biographers.

name: Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah
line: A Makkan woman who walked alone to Madinah after Hudaybiyyah, prompting a verse on women emigrants.
story: Though her father Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt was a bitter enemy of Islam, Umm Kulthum believed and, after the truce of Hudaybiyyah, fled to Madinah on her own. Her brothers came to take her back under the treaty, but Allah revealed that believing women who emigrate are not to be returned to the disbelievers.
note: That 60:10 came in connection with her is reported by al-Bukhari. She was a half-sister of Uthman through his mother.

name: Asma bint Yazid
line: An Ansari woman who spoke up for the women of Madinah before the Prophet ﷺ.
story: Asma once asked the Prophet ﷺ on behalf of the women whether they shared the reward of men who went out to fight and pray in congregation. He turned to his Companions, praised her question, and told her that a woman who keeps her home well equals all of that. She is also reported to have fought at Yarmuk.
note: The 'speaker for women' report is from al-Bayhaqi, and her part at Yarmuk is from later historians; both carry some weakness. She narrated many hadith.

name: Khawlah bint al-Azwar
line: A woman warrior of the Syrian conquests, more famous in legend than in sound history.
story: Later stories tell how Khawlah rode masked into battle to rescue her captured brother Dirar, and how Khalid ibn al-Walid admired the unknown knight before learning she was a woman. These tales made her a heroine for later generations of Muslims.
note: Her story comes mainly from the Futuh al-Sham attributed to al-Waqidi, a later and unreliable work. Early historians say little or nothing of her, so many scholars doubt the details or even her existence.

name: Al-Khansa
line: The greatest woman poet of Arabia, whose elegies for her brother are still recited.
story: Tumadir bint Amr, called al-Khansa, mourned her brother Sakhr in poems of grief known across Arabia. She came to the Prophet ﷺ with her tribe and accepted Islam, and he enjoyed hearing her verse. Later tradition says that when her four sons fell at Qadisiyyah, she praised Allah for honouring her with them.
note: The story of her four sons at Qadisiyyah is famous but comes through weak, late chains.

name: Hind bint Utbah
line: Wife of Abu Sufyan, once a fierce enemy at Uhud, who accepted Islam when Makkah opened.
story: Hind lost her father, uncle and brother at Badr and urged Quraysh on at Uhud. When Makkah opened in 630 she came to pledge to the Prophet ﷺ with the women and spoke boldly during the pledge. She destroyed her household idol and later sent her sons to the campaigns in Syria. Islam erased what came before.
lesson: No past is too dark for repentance.
note: Her words during the women's pledge in 60:12 are reported in tafsir. She was told she may take from her husband's wealth what reasonably suffices her and her children (Bukhari 5364). Her death date is uncertain.

name: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb
line: The leader of Quraysh for years against the Muslims, who accepted Islam the night before Makkah opened.
story: Abu Sufyan led Quraysh at Uhud and the Trench. Trading in Syria, he was questioned by Heraclius about the Prophet ﷺ and answered honestly. On the eve of the conquest in 630 he accepted Islam, and the Prophet ﷺ declared that whoever entered Abu Sufyan's house would be safe. He later fought at Ta'if and Yarmuk.
lesson: Honesty can open the door to guidance, even for an enemy.
note: 'Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe' is reported by Muslim. Death year given between 650 and 653.

name: Wahshi ibn Harb
line: The slave who killed Hamzah at Uhud for his freedom, then repented and fought Musaylimah.
story: Wahshi was an Abyssinian slave promised freedom if he killed Hamzah, and his spear did so at Uhud. After Makkah opened he came to the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam; his past was forgiven, though the Prophet ﷺ asked him to stay out of his sight. At Yamamah he threw the same spear at Musaylimah the false prophet.
lesson: Islam wipes out the sins before it.
note: He tells his own story in Bukhari 4072. Some link 39:53 to him, but that report is weak. He died in Homs; the date is uncertain.

name: Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl
role: Son of Abu Jahl, martyr of Syria
line: The son of Islam's fiercest enemy, who became a believer and died fighting for it.
story: Ikrimah fought the Muslims for years like his father. When Makkah opened he fled toward Yemen, but his wife Umm Hakim, already Muslim, followed him and brought a promise of safety. The Prophet ﷺ received him warmly. He fought in the Ridda wars and fell in the Syrian campaigns in about 636.
lesson: Children are not their parents' sins.
note: Some sources say he died at Ajnadayn in 634 rather than Yarmuk.

name: Khalid ibn al-Walid
line: The general who beat the Muslims at Uhud, became Muslim, and never lost a battle again.
story: Khalid's cavalry charge turned Uhud against the Muslims. He became Muslim in 629, and at Mu'tah months later saved the army after three commanders fell. He led in the Ridda wars and against Persia in Iraq, then crossed the desert to Syria and broke the Byzantine army at Yarmuk. He died in his bed in Homs.
note: The Prophet ﷺ called him 'a sword of the swords of Allah' (Bukhari 3757). His birth year is uncertain.

name: Amr ibn al-As
line: A shrewd Qurayshi who became Muslim in 629 and opened Egypt for Islam.
story: Before Islam, Amr was sent by Quraysh to the Najashi to bring back the emigrants, and failed. He became Muslim with Khalid in 629 and led campaigns in Palestine. In 640 to 642 he took Egypt and founded Fustat, the first Muslim city there, with its mosque still standing in Cairo. He governed Egypt and died there in 664.
note: He was one of the two arbiters after Siffin. His birth year is approximate.

name: Usamah ibn Zayd
line: Son of Zayd and Umm Ayman, made commander of an army at about eighteen.
story: Usamah grew up in the Prophet's household, so loved that he was called 'the beloved, son of the beloved'. In 632 the Prophet ﷺ placed him over an army that included senior Companions, and some objected to his age. The Prophet ﷺ died before it left, and Abu Bakr sent it on as the Prophet ﷺ had ordered.
lesson: Merit, not age or lineage, earns trust.
note: The objection to his command and the Prophet's defence of him are reported by al-Bukhari. Death year given between 673 and 675.

name: Al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin
line: The commander who led the victory of victories at Nahavand and died in it.
story: Al-Nu'man came to Madinah with his tribe Muzaynah and accepted Islam. Umar chose him to lead the decisive battle against Persia at Nahavand in 642. He was killed early in the fighting; his brother hid his death and the army won. When Umar heard, he wept.
note: Nahavand is dated 641 or 642.

name: Uqbah ibn Nafi
line: The general who founded Kairouan and rode his horse into the Atlantic.
story: Born in the Prophet's lifetime, Uqbah grew up in the conquest of Egypt under his relative Amr ibn al-As. In 670 he founded Kairouan in Tunisia, which became the base of Islam in North Africa. Later he marched west until the Atlantic, rode into the waves, and said only the sea stopped him. He was killed near Biskra in 683.
legacy: The Great Mosque of Kairouan still bears his name.
note: He was born around the Prophet's time but narrated nothing from him; scholars differ on whether he counts as a Companion. The Atlantic speech is from later historians.

name: Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan
line: A scribe of the Prophet ﷺ, longtime governor of Syria, and the first Umayyad caliph.
story: Mu'awiyah accepted Islam around the conquest of Makkah and wrote for the Prophet ﷺ. Umar and Uthman made him governor of Syria, where he built the first Muslim fleet. After Uthman's killing he and Ali differed, and they met at Siffin. In 661 Hasan made peace with him, and he ruled a reunited caliphate from Damascus for twenty years.
note: His work as a scribe is reported by Muslim. Sunni scholars regard him as a Companion and hold back from condemning either side of the civil strife.
title: Caliph

name: Abdullah ibn Rawahah
line: An Ansari poet who chanted verses while digging the Trench and died leading at Mu'tah.
story: Abdullah ibn Rawahah pledged at Aqabah and became a poet of Islam. His verses were sung as the Companions dug the Trench. At Mu'tah in 629 he was the third commander, taking the banner after Zayd and Jafar fell, and he too was killed.
note: Commentators name him, Hassan ibn Thabit and Ka'b ibn Malik as the believing poets excepted in 26:227.

name: Abdullah ibn Jahsh
line: The Prophet's cousin whose patrol at Nakhlah in a sacred month brought down a verse.
story: Abdullah, brother of Zaynab bint Jahsh, led a small patrol to Nakhlah to watch a Qurayshi caravan. They fought it on what may have been the last day of a sacred month, and Quraysh cried out. The Quran answered that fighting then was grave, but driving people from the Sacred Mosque was graver. He was killed at Uhud.
note: The link between the Nakhlah raid and 2:217 is from Ibn Ishaq and the commentators.

name: Anas ibn al-Nadr
line: Anas ibn Malik's uncle, who missed Badr, vowed to make up for it, and fell at Uhud.
story: Anas ibn al-Nadr grieved that he had missed Badr and promised that Allah would see what he did next time. At Uhud, as others fell back, he pressed forward saying he could smell Paradise beyond the mountain. He was found with over eighty wounds, known only by his sister from his fingertips.
note: Anas ibn Malik said they believed 33:23 was revealed about him and those like him (Bukhari 2805).

name: Abu Dujanah
role: The man with the red band
line: An Ansari warrior who took the Prophet's sword at Uhud and gave it its due.
story: At Uhud the Prophet ﷺ held up a sword and asked who would take it with its right. Abu Dujanah, Simak ibn Kharashah, took it, tied on his red headband and strutted between the lines; the Prophet ﷺ said Allah dislikes such a walk except in battle. He shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his back and died at Yamamah.
note: The sword at Uhud is reported by Muslim. The remark about his walk is from the biographers. Yamamah is dated 632 or 633.

name: Salim mawla Abi Hudhayfah
line: A freed slave of Persian origin, one of four the Prophet ﷺ named to learn the Quran from.
story: Salim was adopted by Abu Hudhayfah before adoption by name was ended. His Quran was so good that he led the first emigrants in prayer at Quba, including great men of Quraysh. At Yamamah he carried the Muhajirun's banner and was killed beside his old master.
note: That he led prayer at Quba is reported by al-Bukhari. Yamamah is dated 632 or 633.

name: Al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad
line: An early believer whose words before Badr delighted the Prophet ﷺ.
story: Before Badr, when the Muslims faced an army three times their size, al-Miqdad stood and said they would not say what Musa's people said, 'Go, you and your Lord, and fight', but would fight on his right and left. The Prophet's face lit up. He is said to be the only Muslim on horseback at Badr. He died near Madinah around 653.
note: His words before Badr are reported by al-Bukhari. 5:24 is the saying of Musa's people that he refused to echo.

name: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud
line: A poor shepherd boy who became one of the greatest teachers of the Quran.
story: Ibn Mas'ud was among the first six Muslims and is said to be the first to recite the Quran aloud at the Kaaba, for which he was beaten. He served the Prophet ﷺ closely, who once asked him to recite and wept at 4:41. Umar sent him to teach in Kufa, where his students founded a great school of law.
legacy: The Hanafi school traces much of its method to his teaching in Kufa.
note: Reciting aloud at the Kaaba is from Ibn Ishaq. The Prophet ﷺ weeping at his recitation is reported by al-Bukhari.

name: Abdullah ibn Abbas
line: The Prophet's young cousin, for whom he prayed to be given understanding of the Quran.
story: Ibn Abbas was about thirteen when the Prophet ﷺ died. He then went from Companion to Companion, waiting at doors to learn every hadith. Umar seated him among the elders for his insight. He became the founder of tafsir, teaching in Makkah and Ta'if, and is called 'the interpreter of the Quran'.
legacy: Most classical tafsir begins with what Ibn Abbas said.
lesson: Humble persistence turns a young student into a teacher of nations.

name: Abu Hurayrah
line: A Yemeni who came in 628 and in four years memorised more hadith than anyone.
story: Abu Hurayrah of the tribe of Daws reached Madinah around the time of Khaybar. Poor and without family, he lived among the people of the Suffah and stayed by the Prophet ﷺ while others traded or farmed. He narrated over five thousand hadith and later served as governor of Bahrain and of Madinah.
legacy: A large share of the Sunnah reaches us through him.
note: His real name is given as Abd al-Rahman ibn Sakhr, among other suggestions. Death year given as 676 to 679.

name: Abdullah ibn Umar
line: Umar's son, who copied the Prophet's example so closely he would pray where he had prayed.
story: Too young for Uhud, Ibn Umar pledged at Hudaybiyyah and spent his life learning and following the Sunnah. He refused high office and kept away from the civil wars. A great narrator and jurist of Madinah, he gave fatwas for sixty years and died in Makkah in 693.
legacy: His fatwas are a pillar of the Maliki school through his freed slave Nafi.

name: Abdullah ibn Amr
line: Son of Amr ibn al-As, who wrote down hadith with the Prophet's permission.
story: Abdullah became Muslim before his father and was devoted to worship, fasting so much that the Prophet ﷺ told him to fast like Dawud, every other day. He wrote down what he heard, collected in a book called al-Sadiqah. Abu Hurayrah said only Abdullah had more hadith than he, because he wrote.
note: The advice to fast like Dawud is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim. His death year and place are disputed (Egypt, Makkah or Ta'if, 682 to 692).
wiki: Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As

name: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri
line: A young Ansari who became one of the great narrators and teachers of Madinah.
story: Abu Sa'id was turned back as too young for Uhud, where his father was killed. He fought at the Trench and later campaigns, then spent decades teaching in Madinah. He narrated many well-known hadith, including the duty to change wrong with the hand, then the tongue, then the heart.
note: Death year given between 682 and 693.

name: Jabir ibn Abdullah
line: An Ansari narrator who is said to have ridden a month to hear one hadith.
story: Jabir pledged at Aqabah as a boy with his father, who was later martyred at Uhud. At the Trench he invited the Prophet ﷺ to a small meal that fed the whole army. In old age he travelled to Syria to hear a single hadith from another Companion. He was one of the last Companions to die in Madinah.
note: The meal at the Trench is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim; the journey for a hadith is mentioned by al-Bukhari without a full chain. Death year given as 693 to 698.

name: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
line: A Yemeni whose recitation was said to have the sweetness of the family of Dawud.
story: Abu Musa came from Yemen and reached the Prophet ﷺ at Khaybar with the emigrants from Abyssinia. The Prophet ﷺ, hearing him recite at night, said he had been given a flute of the family of Dawud. Umar made him governor of Basra, where he taught the Quran. He was later one of the two arbiters after Siffin.
note: Death year given as 662 or 672.

name: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman
line: The Companion trusted with the names of the hypocrites, and who urged one Quran for all.
story: The Prophet ﷺ told Hudhayfah the names of the hypocrites, and Umar would not pray over a man's funeral if Hudhayfah did not. On the freezing night of the Trench he crept into the enemy camp as a scout. Alarmed by quarrels over recitation in the army, he urged Uthman to unite the Muslims on one copy of the Quran.
lesson: Knowing evil helps you avoid it.
note: The night mission at the Trench is reported by Muslim. He died shortly after Uthman.

name: Abdullah ibn Salam
line: A learned rabbi of Madinah who recognised the Prophet ﷺ and was promised Paradise.
story: When the Prophet ﷺ reached Madinah, Abdullah ibn Salam came, asked questions only a prophet could answer, and believed. He asked the Prophet ﷺ to question his people about him first: they praised him, then reviled him when he declared his Islam. A verse speaks of a witness from the Children of Israel.
note: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said 46:10 was revealed about him (Bukhari 3812). Some commentators hold the verse is Makkan and general.

name: Tamim al-Dari
role: The Christian who sailed to an island
line: A Christian from Palestine who became Muslim and told of meeting a chained man on an island.
story: Tamim came to Madinah in 630 and accepted Islam. He told the Prophet ﷺ of a voyage when a storm drove his ship to an island where he met a strange beast and a chained man who asked about the coming prophet. The Prophet ﷺ gathered the people to repeat the story. Tamim later lived in Palestine.
note: Commentators say 5:106-108 came about a will witnessed by Tamim and Adi ibn Badda while they were still Christians (Reported by al-Bukhari). The chained man is understood to be the Dajjal.

name: Adi ibn Hatim
role: Son of the most generous Arab
line: A Christian prince of Tayy, son of the famously generous Hatim, who became Muslim.
story: Adi fled to Syria when Muslim horsemen came, but his captive sister was freed with honour and urged him to go to the Prophet ﷺ. Meeting him, Adi was struck by his humility. He was told that a woman would one day travel alone from Hira to the Kaaba in safety, and lived to see it. He stayed firm when his tribe was tempted to apostasy.
note: His question about 9:31, that Christians took scholars as lords by obeying them in what they made lawful, is reported by al-Tirmidhi with some weakness. The prophecy of the safe traveller is reported by al-Bukhari.

name: Thumamah ibn Uthal
line: A captured chief who was won over by kindness and cut off grain to Quraysh.
story: Thumamah, chief of Banu Hanifah, was captured and tied to a pillar of the mosque in Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ asked after him for three days and then freed him. Thumamah washed, returned and became Muslim, saying no face had been more hateful to him and now none was dearer. When Musaylimah rose, he stayed loyal.
lesson: Mercy can win what force cannot.
note: His story is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

name: Abu Lubabah
role: The man who tied himself to a pillar
line: An Ansari who felt he had betrayed a trust and tied himself to a mosque pillar until forgiven.
story: During the siege of Banu Qurayzah, Abu Lubabah, their old ally, let slip by a gesture what fate awaited them. Regretting it at once, he tied himself to a pillar of the Prophet's mosque and refused to be untied until Allah forgave him. The pillar is still called the Pillar of Repentance.
lesson: Owning a mistake quickly is the start of repentance.
note: Commentators connect 8:27 or 9:102 with him; reports differ on which, and on whether the pillar story belongs to Qurayzah or Tabuk.

name: Ka'b ibn Malik
role: One of the three who stayed behind
line: A poet who stayed behind from Tabuk without excuse, told the truth, and was forgiven by Allah.
story: When the army left for Tabuk, Ka'b kept delaying until it was too late. On the Prophet's return the hypocrites made excuses, but Ka'b admitted he had none. For fifty days no Muslim spoke to him. Then Allah revealed that the three who stayed behind were forgiven, and Ka'b gave away part of his wealth in thanks.
lesson: Truthfulness saved him where excuses would not.
note: He tells his own story in Bukhari 4418. The other two were Hilal ibn Umayyah and Murarah ibn al-Rabi. Death year given as 670 to 673.

name: Hilal ibn Umayyah
line: An elderly Badr veteran named in two turning points of revelation.
story: Hilal was one of the three who stayed behind from Tabuk and were forgiven in 9:118; being old, he wept for fifty days. He was also the man who accused his wife before the Prophet ﷺ without witnesses, after which the verses of mutual cursing between spouses were revealed.
note: His case and 24:6-9 are reported by al-Bukhari; another report links the same verses to Uwaymir al-Ajlani.

name: Zayd ibn Arqam
line: A young Ansari whose report about the hypocrite chief was confirmed by Surah al-Munafiqun.
story: On a campaign, the boy Zayd heard Abdullah ibn Ubayy say that when they returned to Madinah the 'honoured' would drive out the 'humble'. He told the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Ubayy swore he never said it, and Zayd was doubted until Allah revealed 63:8. Zayd later lived in Kufa and narrated many hadith.
note: Death year given as 685 to 688.

name: Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr
line: The first child born to the emigrants in Madinah, later ruler in Makkah.
story: Born to Asma and al-Zubayr soon after the Hijrah, his birth disproved a rumour that the Jews had bewitched the emigrants to be childless. The Prophet ﷺ chewed a date and placed it in his mouth. He fought in North Africa and later held the caliphate from Makkah for nine years, until he was killed in the siege of 692.
note: His birth and the date are reported by al-Bukhari from Asma. Some date his birth to 622 or 623.

name: Dihyah al-Kalbi
line: The handsome Companion who carried the Prophet's letter to the Byzantine emperor.
story: Dihyah of the tribe of Kalb traded with Syria and knew the Byzantine world. In 628 he carried the Prophet's letter inviting Heraclius to Islam. The angel Jibril sometimes came to the Prophet ﷺ in Dihyah's form. He lived on into the Umayyad period in Syria.
note: Jibril appearing in his form is reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim. His death date is uncertain.

name: Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah
line: A Badr veteran whose secret letter to Makkah was revealed, and forgiven.
story: Hatib carried the Prophet's letter to the Muqawqis, ruler of Egypt, who returned gifts. Before the conquest of Makkah he secretly wrote to Quraysh to protect his family there. Revelation exposed it and Ali caught the messenger. Hatib explained he had not left his faith, and the Prophet ﷺ forgave him, reminding Umar that Allah had forgiven the people of Badr.

name: Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri
line: A daring messenger who carried the Prophet's letter to the king of Abyssinia.
story: Amr ibn Umayyah fought against the Muslims at Badr and Uhud, then became Muslim. He was known for bold, solitary missions. The Prophet ﷺ sent him to the Najashi with letters, including the request to marry Umm Habibah and bring the emigrants home. He lived into the reign of Mu'awiyah.
note: His missions are known from the biographers. His death date is uncertain.

name: Hassan ibn Thabit
line: The poet who defended the Prophet ﷺ with verse, with the Holy Spirit supporting him.
story: Hassan was already a famous poet of Madinah when he accepted Islam in old age. When Quraysh mocked the Prophet ﷺ in poetry, he answered for him from a pulpit set up in the mosque. The Prophet ﷺ prayed that Jibril support him. He is said to have lived about 120 years.
note: Commentators name him among the believing poets excepted in 26:227. His great age is traditional; his death is given between 659 and 674.
